es.q: Discuss spina bifida occulta, including its definition, frequency, location, and the significance of skin markers.
es.m:
- **Definition and structure:** Incomplete closure of the posterior laminar arches without involvement of nervous tissue, representing the hidden form of spina bifida.
- **Frequency and location:** Affects up to about 30% of the population and is most often an incidental radiographic finding at the L5 and S1 levels.
- **Neurological significance:** The condition has no neurological significance by itself.
- **Underlying markers:** Suspect an underlying intraspinal lesion if there is an overlying skin marker present on examination.
- **Types of skin markers:** Markers include a hairy patch (hypertrichosis), dimple or dermal sinus, lipoma, haemangioma, or hyperpigmentation.

es.q: List and explain the three types of open neural tube defects (spina bifida cystica or aperta).
es.m:
- **Meningocele:** A cystic outpouching of meninges with CSF only, featuring an intact spinal cord and a child who is usually neurologically normal.
- **Myelomeningocele (MMC):** The most common and serious form where the sac contains neural tissue (the malformed spinal cord/cauda equina, the neural placode) and meninges, causing lower limb paralysis and sphincter dysfunction.
- **Myeloschisis (myelorachischisis):** The malformed neural tube is splayed open over several segments without meningeal or skin cover.
- **Presentation:** All types of open neural tube defects present at birth with a sac protruding through the defect in the posterior laminae.

ai.title: Spina Bifida
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Spina bifida is a neural‑tube defect from failed closure of the caudal neuropore, presenting as open or occult forms. Early folic acid reduces incidence; management focuses on preventing infection, hydrocephalus and neurogenic bladder.

sections.p: Spina bifida is incomplete closure of the vertebral arches during the 4th–5th week of gestation. It is classified as occult (no skin defect) or open (cystic/meningocele).
b: Open forms expose meninges or neural tissue; occult forms may have a dermal sinus or no skin sign.

t.b: Detects spinal defect and associated hydrocephalus; positive if fluid‑filled sac seen
Defines extent of neural tissue involvement; positive if cord is tethered or herniated
Shows vertebral anomalies; positive if hemivertebrae or spina bifida markers are present

sections.p: Severity is graded by the level and type of neural involvement. The Shapiro classification (I–IV) is commonly used in low‑resource settings.
b: I – mild, no neurological deficit; II – mild deficit, no bladder involvement; III – moderate deficit, bladder dysfunction; IV – severe deficit, bladder and bowel loss

sections.p: The primary cause is folate deficiency during periconceptional period. Other risk factors include maternal diabetes, obesity, certain medications (e.g., valproate), and infections.
b: Infections such as TB, malaria, schistosomiasis

sections.p: Open spina bifida presents with a visible sac; occult may be asymptomatic or show a skin tag. Common symptoms include motor weakness, sensory loss, bladder dysfunction and hydrocephalus.
Investigations aim to define anatomy, rule out infection and assess hydrocephalus.

t.b: Shows extent of neural tissue and hydrocephalus; abnormal if cystic mass or ventriculomegaly
Detects infection or hematuria; abnormal if leukocytes or nitrites present
Abnormal if renal dysfunction from neurogenic bladder; abnormal if creatinine >1.5 mg/dL
Screen for infections that may worsen neurogenic bladder; abnormal if Chlamydia or Gonorrhoea detected

sections.p: Urgent complications include meningitis, hydrocephalus, and urinary tract infection. Red flags are fever, neck stiffness, rapid headache, or worsening neurological status.
b: New or worsening weakness – spinal cord compression

sections.p: Management is multidisciplinary: surgical repair, infection control, hydrocephalus treatment, and bladder management.
b: Folic acid supplementation for mother and child

sections.p: Regular neuro‑developmental assessment, bladder monitoring, and early intervention for hydrocephalus. Prevention hinges on periconceptional folic acid.
Spina bifida occulta may be mistaken for simple back pain or dermal sinus.
b: Back pain from musculoskeletal causes – no neural deficit

sections.p: Normal X‑ray does not exclude occult spina bifida; normal urinalysis may miss early UTI.
b: Urine dipstick may be negative early in UTI

whenToSeekHelp: Urinary retention or incontinence with pain

faq.q: How do you differentiate open from occult spina bifida?
faq.a: Open has a visible sac or meningocele; occult has no skin defect but may have a dermal sinus.

faq.q: Why is early surgical repair critical?
faq.a: It prevents meningitis and reduces risk of hydrocephalus and neurological deterioration.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order for a newborn with a visible sac at the lumbar spine? — Ultrasound to confirm neural tissue and rule out hydrocephalus.
A 2‑year‑old with spina bifida presents with urinary incontinence. What is the next step in management? — Initiate clean intermittent catheterisation and refer for urodynamic study.
A mother of a child with spina bifida reports fever and neck stiffness. What is the most likely complication and immediate treatment? — Meningitis; start empirical ceftriaxone and obtain CSF.
How would you explain the risk of hydrocephalus in a child with spina bifida to a parent? — Hydrocephalus occurs when CSF accumulates due to blockage; it can be treated with a shunt.
What drug should be avoided in a child with neurogenic bladder and spina bifida? — Anticholinergics that worsen bladder emptying.
A patient with spina bifida has a normal X‑ray but complains of back pain. What should you consider? — Occult spina bifida or dermal sinus; consider MRI.
Why is folic acid supplementation important for the mother of a child with spina bifida? — It reduces recurrence risk and supports neural tube closure.
What is the most common site of spina bifida in the spine? — The lumbosacral region.
